findings.title: utm_* keys with malformed percent-encoding are silently dropped from utmData because the occurrence scan decodes keys with decodeURIComponent while queryString.parse decodes with decode-uri-component
findings.spec_requirement: SPEC §5.1 (D4): utmData is "an object holding every other param whose name starts with utm_ (i.e. excluding utm_source and utm_campaign), keyed by its param name, each value sanitized"; mechanism contract "order comes from the raw string, values from the parse". No rule permits dropping a utm_* param that queryString.parse captured.
findings.evidence: app/javascript/shared/lib/utils.js lines ~41-49 (sanitizeTrackingParams key scan): the scan derives each key via param.replace(/\+/g, " ").split("=")[0] then decodeURIComponent with a raw-string fallback on throw. queryString.parse (node_modules/query-string/index.js v6.1.0 line ~153, formatter(decode(key, options), ...)) decodes keys with decode-uri-component, which partially recovers malformed sequences instead of throwing. When the two decoders disagree, the membership filter parsedParams[key] !== undefined (utils.js utmDataKeys filter) fails and the param is dropped from utmData entirely — neither captured nor counted toward the 10-key cap. Verified empirically against the installed query-string 6.1.0: '?utm_%C3%A9%=v' → parse key "utm_é%" vs scan key "utm_%C3%A9%" (mismatch); same for 'utm_a%FE%FF', 'utm_%E2%98%83%E2', 'utm_100%25%E2'. Fully-invalid keys (e.g. 'utm_x%E0%A4%A') and '+'/'%3D' cases match on both paths; the drop occurs only for keys mixing valid and malformed percent sequences. Top-level utmSource/utmCampaign/internalRef are read from parse by fixed literal names and are unaffected.
findings.recommendation: Decode the scanned key with the same decoder parse uses — decode-uri-component (already a direct dependency of query-string, resolvable in node_modules) — instead of decodeURIComponent, so scan keys and parse keys are always identical and the parsedParams membership check cannot spuriously fail. Alternatively have the fallback path also attempt the lenient decode. Add a Jest case with a mixed-validity encoded utm_* key pinning that it lands in utmData.

findings.title: Jest coverage incomplete: no test asserts the per-value sanitization rules (255-char truncation, first-of-repeated-array) apply to values INSIDE utmData
findings.spec_requirement: SPEC §9.6 requires Jest coverage of the sanitization contract; §5.1 (D4) defines the rules as per value — "each value sanitized", i.e. 255-char truncation and first-occurrence-of-array apply to utmData values, not just the top-level utmSource/utmCampaign/internalRef fields. Ghost-test discipline (repo rule 26 analog): every contract rule must be falsified by an implementation that omits it.
findings.evidence: app/javascript/shared/lib/utils.test.js: the truncation test (line 4) and the repeated-param test (line 10) both exercise only top-level utm_source. Every utmData-related test (10-key cap line 15, exclusion line 34, absence lines 41/55) uses short single-occurrence values. An implementation that assigned utmData[key] = parsedParams[key] without calling sanitizeTrackingValue would pass all 8 tests (verified by inspection: no test supplies a >255-char value or a repeated param for a non-utm_source utm_* key). The current implementation (utils.js: utmData[key] = sanitizeTrackingValue(parsedParams[key])) is correct, but the §5.1 per-value rules are unpinned for utmData — a regression there would ship silently.
findings.recommendation: Add two assertions to app/javascript/shared/lib/utils.test.js: (1) sanitizeTrackingParams("?utm_medium=" + "b".repeat(300)) → expect(result.utmData.utm_medium.length).toBe(255); (2) sanitizeTrackingParams("?utm_medium=first&utm_medium=second") → expect(result.utmData.utm_medium).toBe("first").
